title: AI Product Photo and Video Examples | AIVideosUGC
description: Browse AI product photo and video examples: a folding e-bike video ad, plus lipstick, hoodie, handbag and boots shown in new scenes. See how it works.
h1: AI Product Photo and Video Examples, Start to Finish
lead: Follow product examples from a starting photo to a finished image or video. Filter the examples by product category or output format.
card: Fifteen products, from lipstick to a folding e-bike, shown in finished photos and video.
intro: Each example follows one product through a set of photo or video outputs. Browse the complete set, filter by category or format, and open a tool link to try a similar direction with your product.

cases.t: Folding e-bike: a product photo and hinge clip
cases.d: A gray folding e-bike appears in a clean studio view, then a vertical clip shows hands unfolding the frame and inspecting its hinge. The sequence gives shoppers a clear product view and shows how the folding mechanism works.

cases.t: Lipstick: one studio shot becomes a vanity scene and a shade swatch
cases.d: The starting photo was a single coral lipstick on a plain studio background. From it we made a scene on a marble vanity beside a mirror and a fresh flower, and a close-up next to a swatch of the same shade, so shoppers can judge the color before they buy.

cases.t: Hoodie: a product detail becomes a studio fit and a flat lay
cases.d: We started with close views of a plain gray hoodie that show its fabric, hood, drawstrings and pocket. From those details we made a studio fit view and a flat lay on a wooden bench with a beanie and scarf, so shoppers can compare the shape and styling.

cases.t: Water bottle: a lifestyle photo becomes a social feed ad image
cases.d: The starting point was a lifestyle shot of a sage green water bottle on a marble table, with a woman relaxing on a sofa behind it. We asked for a feed ad version: the same bottle closer and larger in the frame, beaded with water, next to fresh limes and a folded towel in warm afternoon sun. The result is a square image sized for Facebook and Instagram feeds, with the headline and price left to add afterward in Ads Manager.

cases.t: Leather handbag: a studio shot placed in a cafe and on the street
cases.d: The starting photo showed a tan leather handbag with a gold clasp on a plain background. From it we made a cafe table scene with a latte and sunglasses, and an image of the bag carried on a sunny street, with the shape, color and clasp kept the same in each.

cases.t: Chelsea boots: shown on cobblestones and by the front door
cases.d: We began with a close photo of brown leather Chelsea boots. From it we made a walking shot on cobblestones in evening light and a quiet scene by a wooden front door under a coat and umbrella, ready for a seasonal campaign.

cases.t: Linen tote bag: a product photo placed in everyday scenes
cases.d: From one photo of a linen tote bag we made a scene beside a coffee cup at a sunny cafe and another with the bag carried next to a city bike. The bag stays the same in each image while the setting changes to suit different shoppers.

cases.t: Sunglasses: a packshot becomes a sunny deck scene and a worn look
cases.d: The starting photo was a pair of dark wayfarer sunglasses on a plain background. From it we made a sunlit deck scene and a street portrait with dark tortoiseshell sunglasses, showing the product in a still life and while worn.

cases.t: Coffee bag: a counter display becomes a cafe scene
cases.d: We started with a photo of a kraft coffee bag with a blank label and a scatter of beans. From it we made a first-batch display on a counter and a single bag staged at a cafe counter, so the packaging can fit wholesale and cafe settings.

cases.t: Silver necklace: shown worn, then up close
cases.d: We began with a photo of a simple silver necklace and a portrait. The Jewelry On Model template showed the necklace worn on a dark top, then a close view of the pendant at the neckline, so shoppers can judge the length and the size.

cases.t: Scented candle: a studio shot becomes living room and spa scenes
cases.d: We began with a white ceramic candle jar and its lid on a plain background. From it we made a living room coffee table scene with books and a knit throw, and a spa-style scene on the edge of a bathtub beside a folded towel.

cases.t: Phone case: a product photo becomes stone and autumn scenes
cases.d: We began with a phone case on a soft blue color block. From it we placed this phone case on a textured stone slab and among fallen autumn leaves. The shape and camera opening stay easy to inspect while the background changes.

cases.t: Blue jacket: a product photo becomes an outdoor fit and fabric view
cases.d: We began with a plain blue jacket. From that photo we made a view of the jacket worn outdoors and a close view of its fabric, so shoppers can compare the fit and material before choosing a style.

cases.t: Yoga mat: a rolled mat becomes a bright room and a stretch pose
cases.d: The starting photo was a teal yoga mat rolled up with its strap. From it we made an unrolled mat in a bright living room and an image of someone stretching on the mat, so shoppers can see the size and the texture in use.

cases.t: Hot sauce: from a plain bottle photo to a taco night ad
cases.d: The starting photo showed a glass bottle of red hot sauce with a blank cream label. From it we made a pouring shot over tacos and a rustic table scene with fresh chili peppers, with the bottle shape and color kept the same in both.

faq.q: Can I use these examples to plan a video for my product?
faq.a: Yes. Upload a sharp shot of your product, choose the 9:16 vertical format and a length of 6, 10, 15 or 30 seconds, then describe the opening scene. For a different opening, run it again with a new description.

faq.q: Why don't the examples include prices or headlines?
faq.a: AI sometimes garbles letters and numbers, so prices, headlines and offers are left for you to add in Canva, CapCut or Ads Manager, where every word and number stays exactly as you type it.

faq.q: What can I learn from the product video examples?
faq.a: Use the examples to compare openings, camera movement, and product framing. Build your own version with a sharp photo, a chosen size, and one clear action.

faq.q: How do I choose between a photo and video example?
faq.a: Use photo examples to plan listing, lifestyle, or detail images. Use video examples when movement or a product action helps explain how the item is used.

overview.h2: How to read a product example
overview.p: Each card shows an example product photo, scene direction, and generated result. Look first at the product's outline, color, closure, label area, and other buying details; then look at the new setting or camera movement. The useful question is whether the result gives shoppers a new reason to understand the same item.

overview.h2: Use the gallery as a starting point
overview.p: These examples show possible directions for your own product. They are prompts for a scene, not a promise that every result will include every prop, hand, reflection, or fold from your photo. Start with the closest product type, borrow its level of detail, and make a separate version when you want another opening or setting.

input_guide.h2: Prepare a source photo that can be compared

items.d: Keep the product in focus, uncropped, and large enough to inspect. For shoes, bags, jewelry, or electronics, photograph every side you expect the gallery to show.

items.t: Keep one product in the frame
items.d: A single item makes it easier to tell whether the shape and color stayed consistent. If two products are the point of the comparison, make that relationship explicit in the description.

items.t: Describe one scene at a time
items.d: Name the place, light, action, and useful framing detail: for example, a coffee bag beside a pour-over brewer on a bright kitchen counter. Save a second action for a new version.
Do not rely on generated lettering for a price, date, headline, or discount code. Keep open space where your message can go, then type the final words after download.

results.h2: What each result can help you decide

items.d: A packshot, close-up, side view, or size cue helps a shopper judge the object before ordering. Use it beside the main image when the shape or materials need more explanation.
A lifestyle scene shows where an item belongs: on a vanity, desk, breakfast table, street, or bath ledge. Choose a setting that makes sense for how the product is used.
A square image can give a scrolling feed a clear product moment and room for your own offer. Add the message in the ad tool so every number stays accurate.
Change one meaningful variable, such as the opening scene or background, and make another job. Keeping the product and the rest of the direction steady gives you a cleaner comparison.
Phone case on a tidy desk beside earbuds and a notebook; a hand picks it up and turns the camera cutout toward the light.
Silver necklace on a dark top at a neckline; move from the worn view to a close view of the pendant so shoppers can judge length and size.
Kraft coffee bag on a kitchen counter beside a pour-over brewer, then at a breakfast table with a mug and croissant.
Teal yoga mat rolled with its strap in a bright room, then unrolled while someone stretches beside a window.
Red hot-sauce bottle on a rustic table with fresh chilies; a pour over tacos gives the clip one clear action.
White candle jar on a living-room coffee table with books and a knit throw, then on a bath ledge beside a folded towel.

after_download.h2: Finish the example before you publish

items.d: Put the downloaded result beside the item you ship. Check color, proportions, logos, labels, buttons, edges, and the number of pieces before a shopper sees it.
Place the price, date, offer, headline, captions, and music in Canva, CapCut, TikTok, Ads Manager, or your usual editor. Type the details yourself to keep campaign wording accurate.
AI-generated people are not customers. Keep the text focused on the product and check the current disclosure guidance for the platform where you post the image or clip.

good: Sellers building a listing gallery from one clear product photo
Small shops that need a few distinct settings for social posts or feed ads
Marketers comparing openings, scenes, or formats for the same product
Products whose use, scale, or setting is easier to understand in a picture or short clip
not_ideal: Exact small lettering, prices, dates, or technical specifications that must be copied without errors
A customer testimonial or review, because generated people are not real buyers
A hidden side or unseen feature; provide a source photo for every view you need to show
